plain_title: Too much coffee, or the headache when you stop
one_liner: Problems from caffeine: intoxication after too much, or withdrawal symptoms like headache and tiredness when stopping.
in_simple_words: Caffeine is the world's most used psychoactive substance, and for most people it's fine. The DSM recognizes two caffeine problems: intoxication, when a large amount causes restlessness, racing heart, insomnia, stomach upset, and anxiety; and withdrawal, when a regular user stops and gets headache, tiredness, low mood, and poor concentration for a few days. Energy drinks and caffeine powders make intoxication more likely. 'Caffeine use disorder' is listed as a condition for further study, not an official diagnosis.
what_it_can_feel_like: Four energy drinks before an exam and I thought I was having a heart attack.
I didn't know the Monday headaches were because I skipped coffee at weekends.
Cutting down slowly over two weeks was the trick. No headache, better sleep.
common_signs: After a lot of caffeine: restlessness, nervousness, racing heart, insomnia, upset stomach, muscle twitches
After stopping: headache, marked tiredness, low mood, irritability, trouble concentrating
Withdrawal starting within a day of the last caffeine and lasting a few days
Symptoms causing real distress or disruption

myths_vs_facts.fact: It's a stimulant with real intoxication and withdrawal syndromes, both recognized by the DSM.

myths_vs_facts.myth: Caffeine withdrawal is just being a bit grumpy.
myths_vs_facts.fact: For regular users, withdrawal headaches and exhaustion can be bad enough to miss work, which is why cutting down gradually helps.

myths_vs_facts.myth: Energy drinks are the same as coffee.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Energy drinks and caffeine powders can deliver very large amounts quickly, which is where most serious caffeine intoxication comes from, especially in young people.

how_common.plain: Most adults use caffeine daily. Intoxication is uncommon but rising with energy drinks; withdrawal symptoms affect a large share of regular users who stop suddenly.
how_common.figure: DSM-5-TR text: around 7% of caffeine users may have intoxication symptoms in a year; about half of regular users report headache on abrupt stopping
how_common.note: Figures from the DSM-5-TR text; need primary citations.

what_helps.plain_summary: Intoxication is managed by stopping caffeine and, rarely, medical care for very high intakes. Withdrawal is prevented by cutting down gradually over a week or two rather than stopping dead; simple painkillers and rest help if it happens. Anyone with anxiety, panic, or insomnia is often advised to reduce caffeine, as it worsens all three. No specialist treatment is needed for most people.
evidence_based_options: Medical care for severe intoxication, especially from powders or many energy drinks
Reducing caffeine as part of treatment for anxiety, panic, and insomnia
self_help_that_supports_care: Knowing how much caffeine is in what you drink
Swapping one drink a day to decaf, then another
No caffeine after early afternoon if sleep is a problem
Avoiding caffeine powders and limiting energy drinks

when_to_reach_out: Get medical help if someone has a racing or irregular heartbeat, chest pain, vomiting, or confusion after a lot of caffeine, especially from powders or energy drinks. Talk to a doctor if caffeine seems tied to anxiety, panic, or insomnia.
is_not: Enjoying coffee daily isn't a disorder. Feeling a bit tired without it isn't withdrawal unless it causes real distress.
hope_note: Caffeine problems are easy to fix. Most people feel better within a couple of weeks of adjusting their intake.

open_questions: Find primary sources for intoxication and withdrawal prevalence.

in_young_people: Energy drinks are heavily marketed to teenagers, and emergency visits for caffeine intoxication in young people have risen. Several countries restrict sales to minors.
across_cultures: Coffee, tea, yerba mate, kola, and guarana are woven into cultures worldwide. Typical intake varies hugely, and what counts as 'a lot' depends on where you are.

sub_sections.title: Caffeine use disorder (Section III)
sub_sections.text: A proposed diagnosis for people who can't cut down despite harm. It's being studied and is not an official diagnosis; see its own card.
